To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the structural changes of mechanoresponsive faceted liposomes can be detected by spatially resolved small angle X-ray scattering in a microfluidic device.
the flow-induced changes of mechanoresponsive liposome's bilayers are spatially resolved and the gradient force is responsible for the structural changes of the liposome.

the average bilayer and mean size of the faceted mechanoresponsive liposome change locally under flow conditions, and that the gradient force is the dominant physical mechanism that provokes structural changes and drug release at stenoic constrictions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the purely physical mechanisms which give rise to a highly efficient drug release at stenosises.
the development of a new class of liposomes, which are capable to respond to a mechanical stimulus, i.e. to a gradient of wall shear stress.
the development of novel liposomal systems for targeted vasodilation at stenotic lesions in atherosclerotic blood vessels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gradient force, which is induced by the flow through a constriction, is a purely physical trigger that induces structural changes of faceted liposomes and, thus, their drug release.
mechanoresponsive liposome systems are a promising tool for the treatment of atherosclerosis and other diseases associated with flow-induced changes in the vessel wall.
the flow-induced structural changes in the liposomes are a result of a combination of shear and hydrodynamic pressure, and the gradient force.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of micro-fluidic devices and small-angle X-ray diffraction is a powerful tool to characterize mechanoresponsive liposome systems.

spatially resolved small angle X-ray scattering combined with microfluidic techniques can be applied to study the structural changes of nanometer-sized mechanoresponsive liposomal systems under physiological conditions.

the combination of micro fluidics and spatially-resolved SAXS allows to study the flow-induced structural changes and related drug release from liposomes of nanometre size in a spatially resolved way.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of micro- and nanoscale techniques allows to understand the physical mechanisms, which govern the drug release from mechanosensitive liposomes.
the flow-induced changes of mechanoresponsive liposome's bilayers are detectable and that they can be used as a tool for the targeted drug release at constrictions.
spatially resolved small angle scattering is an excellent tool to characterize the structure of drug-loaded liposomes under flow conditions in microfluidics.
